query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified FeNiCrMn, the dynamic mechanical response is controlled by a temperature‐ and strain‐rate–dependent transition in dislocation mobility. At moderate conditions, thermally activated dislocation glide dominates, yielding a balanced strength–ductility response; whereas at low temperatures or high strain rates, reduced thermally assisted motion leads to dislocation drag (and possibly localized stress concentrations) that increases apparent yield strength while limiting ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Solidified, Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy with a relatively homogeneous microstructure produced by conventional casting or rapid solidification (without additional thermomechanical processing to refine grain size or introduce precipitates).
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the testing temperature (from moderately high to low) and strain rate (from quasi-static to high-rate regime) while performing mechanical tests.
generation.conditions: Perform controlled tensile and/or compressive tests at multiple temperatures (e.g., room temperature, sub-ambient, elevated) and across a range of strain rates (from 10^(-3) s^(-1) up to 10^3 s^(-1)), ensuring consistent sample microstructure and avoiding uncontrolled defects.
generation.structural_mediator: Dislocation density and mobility, including the transition from thermally activated glide (which benefits ductility) to dislocation drag or localized shear band formation (which enhances strength at the cost of ductility).
generation.mechanism: The atomic-scale chemical inhomogeneity inherent in the solidified FeNiCrMn leads to a spread in local activation energies for dislocation motion. At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, dislocations overcome local barriers via thermal activation, maintaining ductility. At lower temperatures or under high strain rates, insufficient thermal energy results in dislocation drag or stress localization, thereby increasing strength while reducing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Mechanical tests will show that at low temperatures or high strain rates, the alloy exhibits higher yield and flow stress but reduced uniform elongation, whereas at elevated temperatures or low strain rates, lower strengths are accompanied by extended ductility. A consistent transition in the strain-rate/temperature plane supports the role of dislocation mobility as the governing mediator.
generation.baseline: The reference condition is moderate temperature and low strain rate, where thermally activated dislocation glide predominates and produces the known balanced strength–ductility performance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies across the range where the material remains in the same phase and microstructural state (i.e., no phase transformation, twinning, or crack initiation events dominate). It may break down under extreme loading where additional mechanisms (such as deformation twinning or adiabatic shear banding) become active.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thresholds for the transition in controlling mechanism and the quantitative magnitudes of strength/dactility changes are currently uncertain and require experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a batch of solidified FeNiCrMn samples with verified homogeneous microstructure. Perform a series of mechanical tests (tensile and/or compressive) at several controlled temperatures (e.g., 250 K, 300 K, 350 K) and a wide range of strain rates (10^(-3) s^(-1) to 10^3 s^(-1)). Employ in situ methods (such as Digital Image Correlation and in situ electron microscopy) to monitor dislocation motion and microstructure evolution. Correlate measured yield strength and ductility outcomes with observed dislocation mobility characteristics.
measurements: Stress–strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, uniform elongation)
In situ imaging of dislocation motion or localized deformation features
Dislocation density measurements via post-deformation microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, across the temperature and strain-rate range, the observed mechanical performance (strength-ductility changes) does not correlate systematically with the predicted transition in dislocation mobility—or if alternative deformation mechanisms (e.g., twinning, phase transformation) dominate without evidence for a dislocation drag transition—then the hypothesis would be falsified.
